title: Giving Your AI Agent a Wallet
summary: Explore agent wallets, Cloudflare Wallets controls, and x402 payments over HTTP. See what is live, what remains undocumented, and how spending limits work.
body_markdown:
An agent wallet is a scoped balance that an AI agent can spend on its owner’s behalf, within limits the owner sets. It lets the agent pay for APIs, tools and content without ever holding the owner’s card.


You have probably seen an agent do this. It reads the docs, picks the right endpoint, drafts the request, and then stops at a signup form that wants a credit card. The rest of the job lands back on you.


Cloudflare Wallets,[announced on August 4, 2026](https://www.cloudflare.com/press/press-releases/2026/cloudflare-gives-ai-agents-an-identity-and-a-wallet/) , is a concrete example of this idea. This article covers what an agent wallet is, which controls Cloudflare has described, how a payment travels over HTTP, and which questions are still open. It shows where agentic payments are heading. It is not a recommendation to use them in production: the product is early and may change or be withdrawn.


## Key Takeaways


- In Cloudflare’s Wallets documentation, last updated August 19, 2026, the only working feature is reserving a handle at cloudflare.pay, and a reserved handle cannot send, receive or hold funds.
- Cloudflare describes two wallet types: Account Wallets, held by the people who own a Cloudflare account, and Virtual Wallets, which agents use through API keys.
- The announced guardrails for a Virtual Wallet are an allowance, a merchant allow-list and a maximum transaction size, plus a manual override from a human. Neither the announcement nor the docs describes expiry or a revoke API.
- x402 attaches a payment to an ordinary HTTP request by reusing the 402 Payment Required status code, so an agent can pay for one API call without creating an account.
- Reserving a handle is free. No pricing has been published for the wallets themselves.


## Why Handing an Agent Your Card Doesn’t Work


A card number gives an agent far more authority than any single task needs. It has no merchant scope, no per-task budget and no record of which agent spent what. The only way to take that authority back is to cancel the card, which also breaks every other charge on it.


[Agents that browse and act for you](https://blog.openreplay.com/agentic-browsers-introduction/) run into this constantly.[Cloudflare’s announcement](https://blog.cloudflare.com/wallets/) points to two missing pieces: agents have no fixed ID to sign up with, and no payment method of their own. So the agent usually stops and passes sign-up, payment and API keys back to a person. That makes it hard for an agent to test and compare many paid services by itself.


## What an Agent Wallet Is: Account Wallets and Virtual Wallets


An agent wallet separates the money from the authority to spend it. A human holds the funds, and each agent gets a limited slice that it can spend on its own. Cloudflare’s design has two tiers.


Wallet type Held by How it operates


Account Wallet Humans who own or use the Cloudflare account Will top up the balance, hand spending to Virtual Wallets and take money back out; can hold a cloudflare.pay handle


Virtual Wallet Agents Agents use it with an API key; it can’t spend past the cap the Account Wallet owner sets


The[Cloudflare Wallets docs](https://developers.cloudflare.com/wallets/) say the aim of Virtual Wallets is to let an agent work without a person signing off on each step, while putting a hard cap on what it can spend. The announcement says agents will use them to buy APIs, content and MCP tools, the same server-side tools covered in[our guide to the MCP ecosystem](https://blog.openreplay.com/developers-guide-mcp-ecosystem/) .


Most of this has not shipped yet:


Live Announced Not described in the announcement or docs


Reserve one handle per account (free), which publishes a page at` HANDLE.cloudflare.pay` and signs you up for launch notifications Funding, sending, receiving and holding funds; Virtual Wallets; guardrails; manual override; identity for specific agents Wallet pricing, launch dates, expiry, a revoke API, concurrency behavior, how buyers dispute a purchase


The[Wallets FAQ](https://developers.cloudflare.com/wallets/faq/) adds some conditions. Reserving a handle does not guarantee you access to a wallet when it launches. A handle cannot be changed, released or moved once reserved. Cloudflare can reject or reclaim reservations. The press release says full wallet access will arrive “in the coming months,” with no date given.


## What Controls Does an Agent Wallet Have, and What’s Missing?


Cloudflare’s announcement lists three guardrails that an owner sets on a Virtual Wallet, plus a manual override for when an agent reaches its limit. None of them are live. The docs mention only “permissions” and a spending limit, and do not name the individual controls.


Control What it limits What it can’t express


Allowance Total spend Whether that spend was sensible


Merchant allow-list Who the agent can pay Which items or how often


Maximum transaction size Size of each payment Many small payments that add up


Manual override Lets an authorized human raise the limit or approve extra funds When an override should expire


Neither Cloudflare’s announcement nor its documentation describes an expiry date for an agent’s spending authority or an API for revoking it. Cloudflare also says a human will be able to review unusual activity, such as unexpectedly fast spending. That is a stated intention, not a documented control: no trigger or mechanism is published.


## How an Agent Pays: x402 and HTTP 402


[x402](https://x402.org/) is an open protocol that attaches a payment to an HTTP request. It reuses the[402 Payment Required](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/402) status code, which HTTP reserved long ago but never defined in practice.[Cloudflare’s Monetization Gateway post](https://blog.cloudflare.com/monetization-gateway/) describes the flow like this:


1. The agent requests a resource from an endpoint that supports x402.
2. The server replies with 402, including the price and how to pay.
3. The agent pays and tries again, this time including proof that it paid.
4. A facilitator checks the payment, and then the server sends back what was asked for.


Cloudflare’s wallets will settle in stablecoins at first. That is Cloudflare’s choice, not a requirement of x402. The Monetization Gateway itself opened as a waitlist when Cloudflare announced it.


A cloudflare.pay handle also lets merchants see who is paying, because it shows which organization an agent belongs to. The announcement’s example is a research agent at` research.example.cloudflare.pay` . Declaring that identity will be optional for the agent, and each merchant decides whether to treat identified agents differently.


## Who Is Responsible When an Agent Buys the Wrong Thing?


No published source yet says who is responsible when an agent buys the wrong thing. The sources leave three questions open.


**What happens to chargebacks?** The Monetization Gateway post presents stablecoin settlement as having no chargebacks, with funds going directly to the seller. Neither the Wallets announcement nor the docs explain how a buyer disputes a purchase an agent got wrong.


**What does the audit trail record?** A payment log shows what was paid. None of the sources describe a record of *why* the agent chose to pay.


**Who owns the mistake?** It could be the account owner, the agent builder or the merchant. The sources don’t say.


InfoQ’s analysis of the launch adds a structural point: these controls set a budget, but they are not a policy. Each check compares one payment against a fixed number. So none of them can express a rule like “don’t buy the same dataset twice this week,” because that rule depends on earlier payments. InfoQ also raises concurrency. If an agent sends several payments at once, each one might be checked against the full allowance before any of the others has been taken off it, so the total can go over the limit. Cloudflare has not published how the allowance behaves in that case.


## The Wider Race for Agentic Payments


Cloudflare is not the only company building agentic payments: Coinbase’s x402 protocol and Stripe’s Link wallet for agents take different approaches to the same problem. x402 was[created by Coinbase and contributed to the Linux Foundation](https://www.linuxfoundation.org/press/linux-foundation-is-launching-the-x402-foundation-and-welcoming-the-contribution-of-the-x402-protocol) . The[x402 Foundation began operating in July 2026](https://www.linuxfoundation.org/press/linux-foundation-announces-operational-launch-of-x402-foundation-to-standardize-internet-native-payments-for-ai-agents-and-applications) with 40 members.


Stripe has taken the opposite approach. At launch, its[Link wallet for agents](https://stripe.com/blog/giving-agents-the-ability-to-pay) gives an agent a one-time-use card or a Shared Payment Token only after the person approves each spend request. Stripe says it will add user-set limits later. Payments are one layer in a wider stack of agent tooling, alongside setups like[Docker MCP for AI agents](https://blog.openreplay.com/docker-mcp-ai-agents/) and[WebMCP, which lets a site expose its own actions to agents](https://blog.openreplay.com/expose-site-actions-ai-agents-webmcp/) .


## Conclusion


An agent wallet replaces “here’s my card” with delegated authority that has limits. Cloudflare’s version sets those limits per payment, and liability, disputes and concurrency are not documented yet. Until funding and payments ship, the only concrete step available is reserving a handle. In the meantime, if you build agents, work out where your own spending rules should live: in the wallet, or in your application.


## FAQs


Does x402 only work with Cloudflare or with stablecoins?


No. x402 is an open standard for payments over HTTP. Coinbase created it, and the x402 Foundation under the Linux Foundation now governs it. The foundation launched with 40 members, including AWS, Google, Stripe, Visa, Mastercard and Cloudflare. The Linux Foundation says x402 supports payment types from traditional cards to stablecoins. Cloudflare chose stablecoins for its own wallets. The protocol does not require them.


Is HTTP 402 Payment Required an official status code?


Yes, but the specification does not define how it behaves. RFC 9110, the HTTP Semantics specification, lists 402 as reserved for future use, and MDN notes there is no standard convention for it. Browsers and HTTP clients treat it like any other 4xx client error. x402 adds that missing convention: what the 402 response carries, how the client pays, and how it retries with proof of payment.


What is the difference between Cloudflare Wallets and Stripe's Link wallet for agents?


They put human approval at different points. Cloudflare says Virtual Wallets will let agents spend on their own, within an allowance, a merchant allow-list and a maximum transaction size set in advance. At its April 2026 launch, Stripe's Link wallet for agents gives an agent a one-time-use card or a Shared Payment Token only after the person approves each spend request. Stripe says user-set limits will follow.


How do I enforce spending rules that an agent wallet's limits cannot express?


Add a policy check in your own application that runs before the agent pays. Keep a ledger of past purchases so the check can reject repeats, such as buying the same dataset twice in one week. Make the check reserve funds atomically, for example with a database transaction or one payment queue per agent. That stops parallel payments from all passing against the same unspent allowance.
